course.title: Atomic – Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics — Stage 7

unit.title: Place Value and Rounding
unit.blurb: Multiplying and dividing whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000, and rounding to the nearest power of 10 and to decimal places.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Multiply and divide integers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000, using place value.

O2.t: Round numbers to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000 and to a given number of decimal places.

sections.title: Multiplying and dividing by powers of 10

p: When you **multiply by 10**, every digit moves **one place to the left** (it becomes 10 times bigger). × 100 moves two places, × 1000 three places.
When you **divide by 10**, every digit moves one place to the **right**. The decimal point stays still; the digits move.
In 34.5 the 3 means 3 tens. Multiply by 10 and every part is ten times bigger: 3 tens become 3 hundreds, 4 ones become 4 tens, 5 tenths become 5 ones. So 34.5 × 10 = 345.
Each column is worth 10 times the column on its right. Making a number 10 times bigger is exactly 'move one column left'.
Compare 4.7 × 100 = 470 with 4.7 ÷ 100 = 0.047: same digits, same number of places, opposite directions.
Count the zeros: that is how many places the digits move.
× moves the digits left (bigger); ÷ moves them right (smaller).
Fill empty places before the decimal point with zeros, and check the size makes sense.
2.5 × 10 is 25, not 2.50. Think of the digits moving.

p: To round, look at the digit **after** the place you are rounding to. **5 or more: round up.** 4 or less: keep the digit.
4837 to the nearest 100: look at the tens digit 3 → 4800. 6.374 to 1 decimal place: look at 7 → 6.4.
4837 lies between 4800 and 4900. The halfway point is 4850. 4837 is below halfway, so it is nearer to 4800.
The digit after the place you round to tells you which side of halfway you are on. A 5 is exactly halfway (or past it), and by agreement we round up.
The numbers differ by only 0.002, but they lie either side of 3.85, the halfway point.
Find the two possible answers either side of your number.
Look at the next digit to decide which is nearer (5 or more: round up).
Keep the place value: fill with zeros before the decimal point.
